inventionTitles.title: 基于机器学习的人工智能能力
Artificial intelligence capability based on machine learning

address.address1: CCPIT Patent and Trademark Office Co., Ltd

event-title.$: ENTRY INTO FORCE OF REQUEST FOR SUBSTANTIVE EXAMINATION

section.content: Techniques for providing Machine Learning (ML) based Artificial Intelligence (AI) capabilities are described. In one technique, a plurality of AI capabilities are stored in a cloud environment. While the AI capabilities are stored, a request for a particular AI capability is received from a user's computing device. Further, in response to receiving training data based on input from the user, the training data is stored in a lease associated with the user in the cloud environment. In response to receiving the request, the particular AI capabilities are accessed, an ML model is trained based on the particular AI capabilities and training data to generate a trained ML model, and endpoints associated with the trained ML model are generated in the cloud environment. The endpoint is provided to a lease associated with the user.

描述了用于提供基于机器学习的（ML）的人工智能（AI）能力的技术。在一种技术中，在云环境中存储多个AI能力。在存储AI能力的同时，从用户的计算设备接收针对特定AI能力的请求。此外，响应于接收到基于来自用户的输入的训练数据，将训练数据存储在云环境中的与用户相关联的租赁中。响应于接收到该请求，访问该特定AI能力，基于该特定AI能力和训练数据训练ML模型以产生经训练的ML模型，并在云环境中生成与经训练的ML模型相关联的端点。将该端点提供给与用户相关联的租赁。

Artificial intelligence capability based on machine learningTechnical Field

The present disclosure relates generally to Artificial Intelligence (AI), and more particularly, to providing reusable AI solutions to multiple end users.

Background

Artificial intelligence has assisted many users and businesses in providing solutions for everyday tasks. However, it is known that constructing AI-based solutions as a fully managed service requires many months (typically more than a year) for a team of more than 15 people to deliver the AI-based service. Only after this point in time is the end user of the AI-based service provided feedback indicating the value provided by the solution. And this is in the context of AI being a rapidly evolving field and having more than thirty thousand papers published annually. Thus, current techniques for constructing AI-based services are not only time consuming, but also expensive.

The approaches described in this section are approaches that could be pursued, but not necessarily approaches that have been previously conceived or pursued. Thus, unless otherwise indicated, they should not be construed as prior art merely as any of the approaches described in this section qualify as prior art merely by virtue of their inclusion in this section.

Disclosure of Invention

The first embodiment relates to storing multiple Artificial Intelligence (AI) capabilities in a cloud environment. While storing the plurality of AI capabilities, a request for a particular AI capability of the plurality of AI capabilities is received from a computing device of the user. Further, in response to receiving training data based on input from a user, the training data is stored in a lease associated with the user in the cloud environment. In response to receiving the request, accessing a particular AI capability, training a machine-learned (ML) model based on the particular AI capability and training data to generate a trained ML model, generating an endpoint associated with the trained ML model in the cloud environment, and providing the endpoint to a lease associated with the user.

In an embodiment related to the first embodiment, the specific AI capabilities include a pre-trained model, and training the ML model includes fine-tuning the pre-trained model based on training data.

In an embodiment related to the first embodiment, the specific AI capabilities include a framework for training the ML model, and training the ML model includes training the ML model using the framework.

In an embodiment related to the first embodiment, while training the ML model, a plurality of statistics associated with training the ML model are generated and stored in tenancy associated with the user.

In an embodiment related to the first embodiment, the trained conditions of the training of the ML model and the training of the one or more other ML models associated with the lease are stored in the lease associated with the user. The condition is one of a pre-training phase, a training start, training in progress, training failure, or training completion.

In an embodiment related to the first embodiment, a set of access policies associated with a plurality of AI capabilities is stored. Further, the receiving request is performed while the set of access policies is stored. Further, in response to receiving the request, it is determined whether the user has access to the particular AI capabilities based on the set of access policies. Further, retrieving the particular AI capabilities is performed only when it is determined that the user has access to the particular AI capabilities based on the set of access policies.

In an embodiment related to the first embodiment, a list of a plurality of AI capabilities is caused to be presented on a screen of a user's computing device. Further, receiving the request includes receiving an input selecting a particular AI capability from among AI capabilities in the list.

In an embodiment related to the first embodiment, a view request to view a status of a plurality of ML models associated with a rental is received from a computing device of a user. Further, in response to receiving the view request, the status of each of the plurality of ML models is caused to be presented on a screen of the user's computing device. The condition is one of deployed, deleted, being created, or failed (failed).

In an embodiment related to the first embodiment, the user is a first user and the lease is a first lease. Further, a second request for a particular AI capability of the plurality of AI capabilities is received from a second computing device of a second user different from the first user. Further, in response to receiving second training data based on a second input from a second user, the second training data is stored in a second lease in the cloud environment that is different from the first lease and associated with the second user. Further, in response to receiving the second request, the particular AI capabilities are retrieved, a second ML model is trained based on the particular AI capabilities and the second training data, a second endpoint associated with the second ML model is generated in the cloud environment, and the second endpoint is provided to a second lease associated with the second user.

In an embodiment related to the first embodiment, statistics regarding usage of a plurality of AI capabilities by different users associated with different tenants in a cloud environment are generated, wherein for each AI capability of the plurality of AI capabilities, the statistics include one or more of a number of tenants with which the AI capability has been associated, a number of tenants with a particular ML model based on the AI capability and to which the particular ML model is currently deployed, a number of ML models that have been generated based on the AI capability and that have currently deployed, a number of ML models that have been generated based on the AI capability, that have been deployed but that are no longer deployed, or a number of failed training of ML models based on the AI capability.

FIG. 4 is a screenshot of an example user interface provided by a management application depicting a reference to a resource of a selected AI capability in one embodiment;

FIG. 5 is a screenshot of an example user interface provided by a management application depicting a condition of a model in one embodiment;

FIG. 6 is a screenshot of an example user interface provided by a management application depicting a condition of a model in one embodiment;

FIG. 7 is a flow diagram depicting an example process 700 for handling AI capabilities in one embodiment;

FIG. 9 is a block diagram of a basic software system that may be used to control the operation of an example computer system.

Detailed Description

In the following description, for purposes of explanation, numerous specific details are set forth in order to provide a thorough understanding of the present invention. It will be apparent, however, that the present invention may be practiced without these specific details. In other instances, well-known structures and devices are shown in block diagram form in order to avoid unnecessarily obscuring the present invention.

General overview

Systems and methods for providing AI capabilities as "code-less" services are described. In one technique, a user visits a cloud provider that provides AI capabilities, which are either a base model that can be retrained or a framework that is performed to train a new model from scratch. The user selects from among a plurality of AI capabilities via a user interface provided by the cloud provider. User selection of an AI capability, uploading of training data to a user's lease, and user input of one or more values of parameters specific to the AI capability are sufficient to automatically train one or more ML models, automatically select an ML model, and automatically deploy the ML model, all without requiring the user to write code or manually create a training job or deploy a job.

Before an embodiment, a user must interact with the cloud provider's data science component (or "lease") in order to create scripts for the training environment and deployment environment, and create training jobs. Embodiments improve computer-related technology by providing users with AI capabilities that hide the complexity of having to interact with data science rentals. Thus, the number of human errors in developing and deploying a machine-learned (ML) model, the time for developing and deploying an ML model, and the cost of such development and deployment are significantly reduced.

Overview of the System

FIG. 1 is a block diagram depicting an example cloud system 110 that provides AI capabilities to cloud users in one embodiment. The plurality of client devices 102-106 of the user of the cloud system 100 are communicatively coupled to the cloud system 110 via one or more computer networks (not depicted), such as a LAN, WAN, and/or the internet. Examples of client devices 102-106 include desktop computers, laptop computers, tablet computers, smart phones, and wearable devices. Although three client devices are depicted, many client devices may be communicatively coupled to cloud system 110.

The cloud provider provides a cloud system 110 that includes leases for each user or organization of the cloud system 110. Thus, while a single customer lease 120 is depicted, cloud system 110 may support many customer leases, one for each customer. Each customer lease 120 is a collection of cloud resources (including data) made available to the customer and owned and managed by the customer (at least temporarily). The data provided by the customer to cloud system 110 is owned by the customer, rather than by the cloud provider. Examples of cloud resources include one or more virtual machines, network resources (e.g., VPNs), computing nodes for running applications, and database nodes for storing data. The customer may be an individual user or an organization.

A single customer lease may include one or more compartments (such as compartment 122). For example, a customer lease may include a "root" compartment and one or more sub-compartments of the root compartment. A bay is a particular portion of a customer lease that includes a collection of data that is not part of any other bay (e.g., a particular database, ML model, access policy). Different compartments may be associated with different groups of organizations and/or different individuals. For example, if the customer is an organization, one bay may be accessible to the organization's financial team, while another bay may be accessible to the organization's marketing team. Thus, different bays may be associated with different access policies and/or authorized users.

In the depicted example, customer lease 120 includes customer compartment 122. The user operates a client device (e.g., client device 102) and directs the client device to access cloud service portal 112 of cloud system 110. Such directing and accessing may be by an application executing on the client device (referred to herein as a "management application"). The management application may be a native (native) application installed on the client device. Alternatively, the management application may be a web application provided by the cloud system 110 that executes within a web browser installed on the client device. The web application accepts credentials (e.g., a user name and password) from the user and the cloud service portal 112 provides access to the customer lease (or a particular compartment within the lease) to which the user is authorized to access. The granting of access to one or more bays depends on policy 129, which policy 129 may define what an authorized user may access in the root or master bay of a customer lease and what an authorized user may access in each bay within the customer lease. The management application allows authorized users to view and manage resources in the rental/bay, select one or more AI capabilities, and initiate training and deployment of one or more ML models based on policies 129 associated with the users and the rental/bay.

Thus, the user's itinerary is to select training data and then receive endpoints of the trained model for deployment. The user is no longer required to create an ML job to perform model training or model deployment.

Cloud system 110 also includes data science lease 130, wherein one or more cloud resources are provided and managed by one or more other users, such as an administrator of cloud system 110. For example, the data science lease 130 includes training and deployment resources for training a machine-learned (ML) model and deploying the trained ML model, which are described in more detail herein. Data science lease 130 may be a native cloud infrastructure service. The data science lease 130 ingests training data, trains models based on the training data, stores the models in a model catalog, and uses the stored models in reasoning.

AI capability

Cloud system 110 also includes AI-capability provider lease 140, which includes resources generated and provided by an entity different from the customer and optionally different from the provider of data science lease 130. AI-capability provider lease 140 includes AI-capability store 142 and policy 144. The AI capabilities store 142 stores one or more AI capabilities, each of which may include a container mirror and may be selectable by a user. The container image is an unalterable static file that includes executable code that enables the container image to run an isolation process on the IT infrastructure. The image includes the system libraries, system tools, and other platform settings required for the software program to run on a containerized platform, such as a Docker.

FIG. 2 is a screenshot of an example user interface 200 provided by a management application in an embodiment. The user interface 200 includes a reference 210 to AI capabilities that a user may select. AI capabilities are reusable single tenant AI products that address specific issues. AI capabilities cover a wide range of AI products (related to a particular problem area) between disposable solutions (i.e., tailored to a single customer) and fully managed services (i.e., which are sufficiently versatile for multiple customers). Reference 210 to AI capabilities includes references to AI capabilities configured for language, forecasting, speech, vision, document understanding, anomaly detection, and digital assistant.

AI capabilities may be a pre-trained ML model or a framework for training a new model. For either scenario, the user provides (e.g., uploads) training data through the management application. In a scenario where AI capabilities are pre-trained ML models, data science lease 130 trims the pre-trained ML models based on training data to produce trimmed ML models. Trimming involves retraining/trimming the model using training data, training some layers of the neural network (i.e., where other layers are locked), and/or training (e.g., classifying) the head (head) for a pre-trained model. In a scenario where AI capabilities are frameworks, the frameworks include code for creating models, modifying models, incorporating user feedback, performing interactive machine learning, and further optimizing the process using ML techniques.

In one embodiment, data science lease 130 provides a management application with visibility regarding AI capabilities. In this way, the data science lease 130 hides details of where the AI capabilities are stored in addition to performing all training and deployment of the generated ML model.

AI capabilities provider lease 140 also includes a policy 144, which policy 144 indicates which entities (i.e., user/organization/customer leases) are permitted to access AI capabilities (e.g., container mirroring) in AI capabilities store 142. Thus, one of the policies 144 may identify (a) one set of entities that are permitted to access a first AI capability in the AI-capability store 142 and (b) a different set of entities that are permitted to access a second AI capability in the AI-capability store 142. Additionally or alternatively, the policy 144 may identify certain entities that are not allowed to access certain AI capabilities.

In an embodiment, different AI capabilities are associated with different questions defining desired inputs from a user selecting the AI capabilities. Furthermore, different AI capabilities have different pre-existing rules. For example, for AI capabilities related to anomaly detection, there may be a problem with threshold or sensitivity, a request for input regarding target false alarm probabilities, and a request for input regarding training score ratios. Regarding forecasting of AI capabilities as one type, the management application may request three types of files (1) a primary time series file, e.g., regarding sales, (2) an impact data file (e.g., weather, promotional period), and (3) a meta-information file (e.g., size/color of clothing, brand of clothing, doorway show). Regarding vision as one type of AI capabilities, the question may be whether the AI capabilities are to be used for object detection, face recognition, document recognition, and/or detection in images and videos.

In an embodiment, cloud system 110 presents different sets of questions to the user at different times (such as installation time and later during use of the management application). The installation time is the period of time that customer leases are being established. Example questions at installation time include questions about where the user has a network, where the user's lease is located, and where to deploy one or more ML models trained for the user. Example questions at a later time include where the training data is located and what the parameters to adjust are, which are specific to the AI capabilities selected.

In addition to the AI-capability store 142 and the policy 144, the AI-capability provider lease 140 can include metrics regarding AI capabilities in the AI-capability store 142. For example, the metrics may indicate, for each AI capability in the AI capability store 142, (a) a number of customers that have borrowed (check out) or otherwise utilized the AI capability, (b) a number of customers that have currently deployed an ML model based on the AI capability, (c) a number of successful training (across multiple customers) of the ML model based on the AI capability, (d) a percentage of customers that are currently using the ML model after the ML model based on the AI capability has been deployed one month ago, and (e) an aggregate error rate associated with the AI capability.

When a user/client selects and runs an AI capability, the infrastructure to run the AI capability comes from cloud system 110 (e.g., data science lease 130) through an installation process. In response to a user/customer selecting an "install" button or option in the management application, an installation script is run and creates resources, such as data science jobs, data science APIs, etc., in customer tenancy 120 through the development tool. Such resources are deployed through development tools. Terraform is an example infrastructure, i.e., code tool, that allows users to build, change, and versioning both cloud resources and locally deployed resources safely and efficiently. Other examples of development tools include Pulumi, cloud Development Kit, cloud foundation, and Ansible.

Thus, the management application is a component with which the user/client interacts to select and install AI capabilities, specify location data indicating where training data is stored, and initiate the running of the generated ML model. The user of the management application no longer needs to write code to train, test or experiment.

In an embodiment, the AI capabilities include code for performing automated hyper-parameter adjustment. In this way, the user/client does not need to know how to write code for hyper-parameter adjustment. In a related embodiment, the AI capabilities include code for training a plurality of ML models based on different hyper-parameters, validating/testing each of the plurality of ML models, and selecting an ML model that performs best according to one or more criteria, such as accuracy, precision, inference time, and/or training time.

FIG. 3 is a screenshot of an example user interface 300 depicting attributes of AI capabilities provided by a management application in one embodiment. The User Interface (UI) 300 includes a name of AI capabilities ("ABCDEF") selected by the user. The UI 300 also includes a reference 310 to a (user initiated) action for the AI capabilities selected by the user. Example actions include configuring AI capabilities (e.g., specifying computing, network, and I/O requirements; selecting and isolating resources) (e.g., performed by an administrator of cloud system 110 or a provider of AI capabilities), authenticating users seeking access to AI capabilities (e.g., performed by an administrator of cloud system 110 or a provider of AI capabilities), using an AI capabilities training model, retraining a base model of AI capabilities, viewing resources of AI capabilities, and monitoring AI capabilities. Customer monitoring of AI capabilities may include monitoring logs and retrieval metrics (e.g., call volume, time spent training/reasoning, model accuracy, loss function).

FIG. 4 is a screenshot of an example user interface 400 provided by a management application depicting a reference 410 to a resource of a selected AI capability in one embodiment. In this example, data about the same AI capabilities as in fig. 3 is displayed. A "resource view" action is selected from the actions listed in fig. 3. Three types of resources are listed, computing resources, model resources, and cluster resources. Model resources are the base model that is trained based on the selected AI capabilities. The computing resources are used to train the model, while the cluster resources are used to keep AI capabilities active.

Data science leasing

An example of a training resource in the data science lease 130 is a training instance 132 that is responsible for training the ML model based on training data provided by a user. Data science lease 130 can automatically initiate (bring up) or generate training instance 132 in response to receiving an indication of the user's selected AI capabilities and corresponding training data. Once training instance 132 completes the training process, data science lease 130 can automatically delete (or "tear down") training instance 132.

An example of a deployment resource that data science lease 130 includes is a resource that automatically generates an endpoint for a trained ML model and associates the endpoint with a customer lease that initiates training of the ML model. An example of an endpoint is a Uniform Resource Locator (URL). Like training instance 132, inference engine cluster 134 (which invokes or evokes the trained ML model) also executes in data science lease 130. The inference engine cluster 134 includes multiple computing machines working together to handle individual machine failures and transfer loads.

Customer leasing assembly

Customer lease 120 includes a number of components including training log 124, input data bucket 126, output data bucket 128, and policy 129. Thus, each of these components is thus accessible to the user of customer lease 120. Training log 124 includes data describing the progress and/or status of one or more model trains. Training instance 132 (in data science lease 130) may generate data that is ultimately stored in training log 124. Thereafter, the user of customer lease 120 may view training log 124 to determine the status of training the ML model based on the user-selected AI capabilities. Example training conditions may include "pre-training phase", "training start", "training in progress", "training failure" and "training complete".

The input data store 126 stores training data for training one or more ML models by training instances 132. The training data includes a plurality of training instances, each training instance including a plurality of values (each value corresponding to a different feature of the model) and a label, such as a class value, an integer, or a floating point value.

The output data store 128 stores statistical data generated during model reasoning. Examples of statistical data include when a particular model was evoked, who caused or initiated the evoked (e.g., a client device located remotely from cloud system 110), whether the evoked particular model resulted in any errors, the time elapsed from the model evoked to the model output for each model evoked, and statistical data about the model output distribution (e.g., percentage of model output in one output class versus another output class; histogram of real value output). If a customer is associated with multiple active ML models, output data store 128 may store statistics for the multiple ML models. Thus, each statistic will include model identification data that identifies the ML model with which the statistic is associated. In a related embodiment, each bay within customer lease 120 is associated with a different output data bucket that stores statistics about the ML model associated with that bay.

The statistics in the output data bucket 128 may be used for diagnostic purposes or to measure model performance. For example, if the number of errors is greater than a certain threshold number or a certain threshold percentage of model calls, then retraining may be automatically triggered and/or the user automatically notified, such as through an email, text message, or software application channel.

Policy 129 defines access policies, in particular who can access which data. For example, a policy may indicate that a particular user (or any user) associated with customer lease 120 is able to access data science lease 130 and AI capability provider lease 140. Thus, policy 129 may allow a customer to initiate one or more operations, such as loaning/utilizing AI capabilities from AI capability provider lease 140, running a job in data science lease 130, and deploying a trained ML model. At least some of the policies 129 may be automatically generated such that a user of the cloud system 110 does not need to learn how to configure the relevant policies. Even with automatically generated policies, policies 129 may include customer-specified policies that may add restrictions or remove restrictions on who may access certain data and/or initiate certain operations.

In one embodiment, customer lease 120 includes a virtual cloud network that provides network isolation. Within customer lease 120, a user may create a Virtual Cloud Network (VCN) for an organization or group of users. VCNs are useful in a security context. For example, a highly restricted customer (e.g., a bank or national defense) may wish to use one or more AI capabilities. Customers may create VCNs that will isolate them from the entire internet in a secure state and limit users that can access and alter the AI capabilities utilized by preventing network access entirely.

Through AI capabilities, different cloud infrastructure resources are directly owned and managed by the user/client, such as management applications (which survive in virtual machines), training logs 124, one or more object stores, VPNs, and the like. In contrast, training, deployment, and reasoning are lifecycles owned and managed by data science lease 130. The user/client need not know how or when to launch cloud resources associated with the lifecycle, nor need it know when to turn them off. Prior to the embodiment, the user/client had to be very familiar with this lifecycle, including writing code for each AI capability.

Model condition

FIG. 5 is a screenshot of an example user interface 500 provided by a management application depicting a condition of a model in an embodiment. UI 500 includes a table identifying nine models, a condition for each model, and a timestamp of creation of each model. Conditions include deployed, deleted (meaning the model has been created/trained at some point in time), being created (meaning the model is currently being trained or validated), and failed (meaning the model produces incorrect output). Data science lease 130 can automatically disable deactivate the failed model. Additionally or alternatively, the user (by providing input via the management application) may deactivate the failed model and/or the deployed model. In addition, the user operating the management application may "cancel delete (undelete)" the deleted model and reactivate the model. Such user input may be received by a user selecting one of the listed models through UI 500.

In the example of fig. 5, nine models are associated with a particular bay (e.g., root bay) within a customer lease (e.g., customer lease 120) that may include multiple bays. To view the models associated with the different compartments, the user (assuming authorization) selects a drop-down menu 510, which drop-down menu 510, when selected, causes a list of compartments to be displayed. User selection of one of those compartments will cause UI 500 to be updated to list the model associated with the selected compartment.

UI 500 also includes view options 502 and 504. The view option 502 may be a default view option to view all models associated with the compartment, regardless of whether the models have been deployed or deployed.

FIG. 6 is a screenshot of an example user interface 600 provided by a management application depicting a condition of a model in an embodiment. UI 600 is the result of a user selecting view option 504 in UI 500. UI 600 indicates that there are three models that have been deployed, are deployed, or are to be deployed. The first two listed models in UI 600 are listed in UI 500. If the form in UI 500 has one additional row, then the third listed model in UI 600 will be listed in UI 500.

In an embodiment, using the management application, a user may provide input that organizes two or more AI capabilities in a sequence or directed graph. For example, the user selects two AI capabilities, a first AI capability associated with Anomaly Detection (AD) and a second AI capability associated with forecast. The user provides a further input indicating that the output based on the output (of the AD model to be trained based on the first AI capabilities) is an input to the predictive model to be trained based on the second AI capabilities. Thus, the AD model "cleans up" the input data by removing outliers or anomalies in the input data, which is then input to the forecasting model. In this way, two or more AI capabilities can be stitched together.

Example processing

Fig. 7 is a flow diagram depicting an example process 700 for handling AI capabilities in an embodiment. Process 700 is performed by one or more components of cloud system 110.

At block 710, a plurality of AI capabilities are stored in a cloud environment. AI capabilities may have been defined by a set of one or more administrators of cloud system 110 and stored in a particular location accessible to multiple users of cloud system 110. AI capabilities may be stored in AI capabilities store 142.

At block 720, a request for a particular AI capability is received while the AI capability is stored. The request may be received from a client device (e.g., client device 102) over a computer network, such as the internet. Block 720 may involve the management application executing on the client device 102 presenting a list of a plurality of AI capabilities from which to select. The management application may access AI-capability store 142 directly or indirectly through data science lease 130. The management application may present only those AI capabilities to which the requesting user has access according to policy 144.

At block 730, training data is received from a user. Block 730 may involve receiving input from a user specifying a storage location where training data is stored (e.g., in a user interface of a management application) and instructions to upload the training data to a cloud environment when the training data is not already located in the cloud environment. Block 730 may also involve storing the received training data in a lease associated with the user in the cloud environment. An example of a rental of a user is customer rental 120. Block 730 may be performed before or after block 720.

At block 740, in response to receiving the request, a particular AI capability is accessed. The specific AI capabilities may be a pre-trained ML model or a framework for training a new ML model. If the access authorization check is not performed in block 720, block 740 may involve checking one or more of the policies 144 associated with the particular AI capabilities to determine whether the user is authorized to use or utilize the particular AI capabilities.

At block 750, a new ML model is trained based on the particular AI capabilities and training data. Block 750 is performed without requiring any code or data from the user creating the training job. Instead, the training instance within data science lease 130 trains a new ML model on behalf of the user. Block 750 may also involve prompting the user for one or more inputs based on the requested AI capabilities prior to training the ML model. Different AI capabilities may be associated with different cues/questions.

Block 750 may also involve generating status data or other statistical data about the training, such as when the training began, when verification began (if applicable), what the current stage of training was, one or more correctness metrics of one or more trained ML models, and so forth. Such data may be available for lease by the user initiating the training.

At block 760, an endpoint is generated in the cloud environment, wherein the endpoint is associated with the ML model. An endpoint is a network location where one or more users can utilize or evoke an ML model. The endpoints may be public or private to the user/client that initiated the generation of the ML model.

At block 770, the endpoint is provided to a lease (e.g., customer lease 120) associated with the user. The user may incorporate the endpoint into a model pipeline, which may include multiple ML models, some of which receive as input an output from another model in the pipeline.

Hardware overview

According to one embodiment, the techniques described herein are implemented by one or more special purpose computing devices. The special purpose computing device may be hardwired to perform the techniques, or may include a digital electronic device, such as one or more Application Specific Integrated Circuits (ASICs) or Field Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs), that are permanently programmed to perform the techniques, or may include one or more general purpose hardware processors programmed to perform the techniques in accordance with program instructions in firmware, memory, other storage, or a combination. Such special purpose computing devices may also incorporate custom hard-wired logic, ASICs, or FPGAs in combination with custom programming to implement the techniques. The special purpose computing device may be a desktop computer system, portable computer system, handheld device, networking device, or any other device that incorporates hardwired and/or program logic to implement these techniques.

For example, FIG. 8 is a block diagram that illustrates a computer system 800 upon which an embodiment of the invention may be implemented. Computer system 800 includes a bus 802 or other communication mechanism for communicating information, and a hardware processor 804 coupled with bus 802 for processing information. The hardware processor 804 may be, for example, a general purpose microprocessor.

Computer system 800 also includes a main memory 806, such as a Random Access Memory (RAM) or other dynamic storage device, coupled to bus 802 for storing information and instructions to be executed by processor 804. Main memory 806 also may be used for storing temporary variables or other intermediate information during execution of instructions to be executed by processor 804. Such instructions, when stored in a non-transitory storage medium accessible to the processor 804, cause the computer system 800 to be a special purpose machine that is customized to perform the operations specified in the instructions.

Computer system 800 also includes a Read Only Memory (ROM) 808 or other static storage device coupled to bus 802 for storing static information and instructions for processor 804. A storage device 810, such as a magnetic disk, optical disk, or solid state drive, is provided and coupled to bus 802 for storing information and instructions.

Computer system 800 may be coupled via bus 802 to a display 812, such as a Cathode Ray Tube (CRT), for displaying information to a computer user. An input device 814, including alphanumeric and other keys, is coupled to bus 802 for communicating information and command selections to processor 804. Cloud computing

The term "cloud computing" is used generically herein to describe a computing model that enables on-demand access to a shared pool of computing resources, such as computer networks, servers, software applications, and services, and that allows resources to be quickly provided and released with minimal administrative effort or service provider interaction.

Cloud computing environments (sometimes referred to as cloud environments or clouds) may be implemented in a variety of different ways to best suit different requirements. For example, in a public cloud environment, the underlying computing infrastructure is owned by an organization that makes its cloud services available to other organizations or the general public. Instead, private cloud environments are typically used by or within only a single organization. The community cloud is intended to be shared by several organizations within the community, while the hybrid cloud includes two or more types of cloud (e.g., private, community, or public) that are bound together by data and application portability.

In general, cloud computing models enable some of those responsibilities that might have been previously provided by an organization's own information technology department to be delivered instead as a service layer within the cloud environment for use by consumers (either inside or outside the organization, depending on the public/private nature of the cloud). The exact definition of components or features provided by or within each cloud service layer may vary depending on the particular implementation, but common examples include software as a service (SaaS) where a consumer uses software applications running on the cloud infrastructure while the SaaS provider manages or controls the underlying cloud infrastructure and applications. Platform as a service (PaaS), where consumers can use the software programming language and development tools supported by the PaaS provider to develop, deploy, and otherwise control their own applications while the PaaS provider manages or controls other aspects of the cloud environment (i.e., everything in the runtime execution environment). Infrastructure as a service (IaaS), wherein a consumer can deploy and run any software application, and/or provide processes, storage, networking, and other underlying computing resources, while the IaaS provider manages or controls the underlying physical cloud infrastructure (i.e., everything below the operating system layer). A database as a service (DBaaS) in which a consumer uses a database server or database management system running on a cloud infrastructure while DbaaS providers manage or control underlying cloud infrastructure, applications, and servers, including one or more database servers.
